<script type="application/json" id="pack-y1w12">{"year":1,"week":12,"id":"y1w12","title":"Relations, Functions and Mapping Rules","subtitle":"Ordered pairs, mapping diagrams, tables and graphs; domain, co-domain and range; types of relations; functions and the vertical line test; linear and exponential mapping rules.","family":"algebra","section":{"no":2,"name":"Algebra","strand":"Algebraic Reasoning","from":9,"to":12},"outcomes":["Represent a relation as ordered pairs, a mapping diagram, a table and a graph.","Identify the domain, co-domain and range of a relation.","Classify relations as one-to-one, many-to-one, one-to-many or many-to-many, and decide whether a relation is a function.","Evaluate functions and find linear rules from points or tables.","Recognise and use simple exponential mapping rules."],"keywords":["relation","ordered pair","mapping diagram","domain","co-domain","range","function","one-to-one","many-to-one","vertical line test","gradient","exponential"],"notes":[{"title":"What is a relation?","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"A **relation** connects elements of one set (the inputs) to elements of another set (the outputs). We can show it as **ordered pairs** $(\\text{input},\\ \\text{output})$, an arrow (mapping) diagram, a table, a graph or a rule. Order matters: $(2,5)$ is not the same as $(5,2)$."},{"k":"box","kind":"definition","title":"Domain, co-domain and range","blocks":[{"k":"ul","items":["The **domain** is the set of inputs.","The **co-domain** is the set of possible outputs that has been declared.","The **range** is the set of outputs actually reached. The range is a subset of the co-domain."]}]},{"k":"p","text":"For $R=\\{(1,2),\\ (2,4),\\ (3,6)\\}$: the domain is $\\{1,2,3\\}$ and the range is $\\{2,4,6\\}$."},{"k":"fig","id":"w12-domain","caption":"The co-domain is $\\{2,4,6,8,10\\}$, but only $2,4,6,8$ receive arrows, so the range is $\\{2,4,6,8\\}$."}],"figs":["w12-domain"]},{"title":"Types of relations","blocks":[{"k":"ul","items":["**One-to-one:** each input has one output, and different inputs have different outputs.","**Many-to-one:** each input has one output, but some inputs share an output.","**One-to-many:** at least one input has more than one output.","**Many-to-many:** several inputs share outputs **and** some inputs have more than one output."]},{"k":"fig","id":"w12-types","caption":"One-to-one and many-to-one relations are functions. One-to-many and many-to-many relations are not, because an input has more than one output."}],"figs":["w12-types"]},{"title":"Functions","blocks":[{"k":"box","kind":"definition","title":"Function","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"A **function** is a relation in which **every** input in the domain has **exactly one** output."}]},{"k":"p","text":"Two different inputs may give the same output (many-to-one is allowed), but one input may never give two different outputs."},{"k":"p","text":"We often write a function as $f(x)$, read “$f$ of $x$”. For $f(x)=2x+1$:"},{"k":"math","tex":"f(3)=2(3)+1=7"},{"k":"p","text":"The output $7$ is called the **image** of $3$, and we can write $3\\mapsto7$."},{"k":"box","kind":"key","title":"The vertical line test","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"A graph shows $y$ as a function of $x$ if **no vertical line** cuts it more than once. A circle fails the test; a straight line that is not vertical passes it."}]},{"k":"fig","id":"w12-vlt","caption":"The parabola $y=x^2$ passes the vertical line test; the circle does not."}],"figs":["w12-vlt"]},{"title":"Mapping diagrams","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"Draw two ovals: the domain on the left and the co-domain on the right. Draw one arrow from each input to its output."},{"k":"ul","items":["For a function, every input has **exactly one** arrow.","An element of the co-domain may receive no arrow, or several arrows."]}],"figs":[]},{"title":"Evaluating functions and inverse relations","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"To evaluate $f(-2)$, replace **every** $x$ by $(-2)$, using brackets:"},{"k":"math","tex":"f(x)=x^2-3x\\quad\\Longrightarrow\\quad f(-2)=(-2)^2-3(-2)=4+6=10"},{"k":"box","kind":"warn","title":"Use brackets for negative inputs","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"$(-2)^2=4$, but $-2^2=-4$. Always put a negative input in brackets."}]},{"k":"p","text":"The **inverse relation** swaps the coordinates of every ordered pair. The inverse of a function is **not always** a function: if two inputs share an output, the inverse gives that output two images."}],"figs":[]},{"title":"Linear mapping rules","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"A **linear** rule $y=mx+c$ has a constant rate of change: when the inputs go up in equal steps, the outputs change by equal amounts."},{"k":"box","kind":"formula","title":"Finding a linear rule from two points","blocks":[{"k":"math","tex":"m=\\frac{y_2-y_1}{x_2-x_1}\\qquad(x_2\\neq x_1)"},{"k":"p","text":"Then substitute one point into $y=mx+c$ to find $c$."}]},{"k":"p","text":"The $y$-intercept of $y=mx+c$ is $(0,c)$. In real situations it is often a starting value, such as a fixed fee."}],"figs":[]},{"title":"Exponential mapping rules","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"An **exponential** rule multiplies the output by the same number (the **common ratio**) each time the input goes up by 1:"},{"k":"math","tex":"y=a\\,r^{x}"},{"k":"p","text":"Here $a$ is the value when $x=0$ and $r$ is the common ratio. For $y=3(2^x)$: $x=0,1,2,3$ gives $y=3,6,12,24$."},{"k":"fig","id":"w12-linexp","caption":"The linear rule adds the same amount each step; the exponential rule multiplies by the same amount, so it grows faster and faster."},{"k":"box","kind":"tip","title":"Difference or ratio?","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"Look at the outputs for equally spaced inputs."},{"k":"ul","items":["Constant **difference** ($3,6,9,12$: add 3) means linear.","Constant **ratio** ($3,6,12,24$: multiply by 2) means exponential."]}]}],"figs":["w12-linexp"]},{"title":"Graphs and modelling","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"Plot $(x,y)$ by moving $x$ units across and then $y$ units up or down. Join the points with a line only when the situation is continuous; for whole-number inputs (such as numbers of people) plot separate points."},{"k":"box","kind":"warn","title":"Common mistakes","blocks":[{"k":"ul","items":["A relation is not automatically a function.","The range is the set of outputs actually reached, not the whole co-domain.","If two pairs have the same first coordinate but different second coordinates, the relation is not a function. The vertical line $x=4$ is a relation but not a function of $x$."]}]}],"figs":[]}],"examples":[{"title":"Domain, co-domain and range","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"The relation $R$ from $A=\\{1,2,3,4\\}$ to $B=\\{2,4,6,8,10\\}$ is $R=\\{(1,2),(2,4),(3,6),(4,8)\\}$. State the domain, co-domain and range, and say whether $R$ is a function."}],"steps":["The inputs (first coordinates) give the domain $\\{1,2,3,4\\}$.","The declared set of outputs is the co-domain $B=\\{2,4,6,8,10\\}$.","The outputs actually used give the range $\\{2,4,6,8\\}$.","Each input appears exactly once, so each has exactly one image."],"answer":"Domain $\\{1,2,3,4\\}$; co-domain $\\{2,4,6,8,10\\}$; range $\\{2,4,6,8\\}$. $R$ is a function.","figs":[]},{"title":"Is it a function?","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"Is $R=\\{(1,3),(2,5),(2,7),(4,9)\\}$ a function? Give a reason."}],"steps":["The connections are $1\\mapsto3$, $2\\mapsto5$, $2\\mapsto7$ and $4\\mapsto9$.","The input $2$ has two different outputs, $5$ and $7$.","A function must give exactly one output for each input."],"answer":"No. The input $2$ has two images.","figs":[]},{"title":"Evaluating a function","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"Let $f(x)=2x^2-3x+1$. Find $f(-2)$ and $f(3)$, and the values of $x$ for which $f(x)=1$."}],"steps":["$f(-2)=2(-2)^2-3(-2)+1=8+6+1=15$.","$f(3)=2(3)^2-3(3)+1=18-9+1=10$.","$f(x)=1$: $2x^2-3x+1=1$, so $2x^2-3x=0$.","Factorise: $x(2x-3)=0$, so $x=0$ or $x=\\dfrac{3}{2}$."],"answer":"$f(-2)=15$; $f(3)=10$; $f(x)=1$ when $x=0$ or $x=\\dfrac{3}{2}$.","figs":[]},{"title":"A linear rule from two points","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"A linear mapping passes through $(0,4)$ and $(2,8)$. Find the rule $y=mx+c$ and the image of $7$."}],"steps":["$m=\\dfrac{8-4}{2-0}=\\dfrac{4}{2}=2$.","The point $(0,4)$ gives $c=4$, so $y=2x+4$.","Image of 7: $y=2(7)+4=18$."],"answer":"$y=2x+4$; the image of 7 is 18.","figs":[]},{"title":"A linear rule from a table","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"For $x=1,2,3,4$ the outputs are $y=7,10,13,16$. Show that the mapping is linear and find its rule."}],"steps":["The inputs go up by 1, and the outputs go up by 3 each time: $10-7=13-10=16-13=3$.","So $m=3$ and $y=3x+c$.","Using $(1,7)$: $7=3+c$, so $c=4$.","Check: $3(4)+4=16$ ✓."],"answer":"$y=3x+4$","figs":[]},{"title":"An exponential rule","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"A savings balance follows the table $x=0,1,2,3$ and $y=5,10,20,40$. Find the rule and predict $y$ when $x=5$."}],"steps":["Ratios: $\\dfrac{10}{5}=\\dfrac{20}{10}=\\dfrac{40}{20}=2$, a constant ratio.","Use $y=ar^x$ with $r=2$. When $x=0$, $y=a=5$.","So $y=5(2^x)$.","When $x=5$: $y=5\\times2^5=5\\times32=160$."],"answer":"$y=5(2^x)$; $y=160$ when $x=5$.","figs":[]},{"title":"The inverse of a function","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"Is $\\{(-1,1),(0,0),(1,1)\\}$ a function? Is its inverse relation a function?"}],"steps":["The inputs $-1$, $0$ and $1$ each appear once, so it is a function (many-to-one).","The inverse swaps the coordinates: $\\{(1,-1),(0,0),(1,1)\\}$.","In the inverse the input $1$ has two outputs, $-1$ and $1$."],"answer":"The relation is a function, but its inverse is not.","figs":[]},{"title":"Printing costs","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"A printing shop charges a fixed fee plus a fixed amount per page. 10 pages cost GH₵35 and 25 pages cost GH₵65. Find a linear rule for the cost and the cost of 40 pages."}],"steps":["Let $x$ be the number of pages and $C$ the cost in cedis: $C=mx+c$.","$m=\\dfrac{65-35}{25-10}=\\dfrac{30}{15}=2$ cedis per page.","Using $(10,35)$: $35=20+c$, so $c=15$ (the fixed fee).","$C=2x+15$, and for 40 pages $C=80+15=95$.","Check: $2(25)+15=65$ ✓."],"answer":"$C=2x+15$; 40 pages cost GH₵95.","figs":[]}],"summary":[{"title":"Key results for Week 12","items":["Domain: inputs. Co-domain: possible outputs. Range: outputs actually reached.","A function gives **exactly one** output for every input.","Vertical line test: no vertical line meets the graph more than once.","Linear rule: $y=mx+c$ with $m=\\dfrac{y_2-y_1}{x_2-x_1}$.","Exponential rule: $y=ar^x$ ($a$ = value at $x=0$, $r$ = common ratio)."]}],"quiz":[{"q":"Which relation is **not** a function?","options":["$\\{(1,2),(2,3)\\}$","$\\{(1,3),(1,4)\\}$","$\\{(1,2),(2,2)\\}$","$\\{(0,0),(1,1)\\}$"],"correct":1,"explain":"In $\\{(1,3),(1,4)\\}$ the input 1 has two outputs."},{"q":"For $f(x)=3x-2$, find $f(4)$.","options":["$14$","$8$","$10$","$-10$"],"correct":2,"explain":"$f(4)=3(4)-2=10$."},{"q":"The co-domain is $\\{2,4,6,8\\}$ and the outputs reached are $2$ and $6$. Many-to-one functions do share outputs."},{"q":"A one-to-many relation is not a function because","options":["its graph is always curved","its co-domain is empty","some outputs repeat","one input has several outputs"],"correct":3,"explain":"A function cannot give one input more than one image."},{"q":"The point $(3,11)$ lies on $y=ax+2$. Find $a$.","options":["$a=2$","$a=3$","$a=9$","$a=11$"],"correct":1,"explain":"$11=3a+2$, so $3a=9$ and $a=3$."},{"q":"For $f(x)=x^2$, which two different inputs have the same output?","options":["$0$ and $1$","$2$ and $3$","$-2$ and $2$","$1$ and $2$"],"correct":2,"explain":"$(-2)^2=4$ and $2^2=4$."}],"exercise":[{"q":"State the domain and range of $R=\\{(-2,4),(-1,1),(0,0),(1,1)\\}$. Yes: each input appears once (it is many-to-one)."},{"q":"For $f(x)=2x^2-5$, find $f(-3)$ and solve $f(x)=13$.","a":"$f(-3)=13$; $2x^2=18$, so $x=\\pm3$."},{"q":"Find the linear rule through $(-1,-2)$ and $(3,10)$.","a":"$m=\\dfrac{12}{4}=3$; $-2=-3+c$, so $y=3x+1$."},{"q":"For $x=0,1,2,3$ the outputs are $3,\\ 9,\\ 27,\\ 81$. List its ordered pairs. Is it a function?","a":"$(2,4),(2,6),(3,6),(3,9)$. Not a function: 2 (and 3) each have two images."},{"q":"Complete the table of $y=2^x$ for $x=0,1,2,3,4$. Is the rule linear?","a":"$1,\\ 2,\\ 4,\\ 8,\\ 16$. The differences $1,2,4,8$ are not constant, so it is not linear; the constant ratio 2 shows it is exponential."}],"theory":[{"q":"Use $R=\\{(1,4),(2,4),(3,9)\\}$ from $A=\\{1,2,3\\}$ to $B=\\{4,9,16\\}$ to explain the difference between domain, co-domain and range.","steps":["Domain (inputs): $\\{1,2,3\\}$.","Co-domain (declared outputs): $B=\\{4,9,16\\}$.","Range (outputs reached): $\\{4,9\\}$; $16$ is never reached.","Each input has one image, so $R$ is a function, even though 1 and 2 share the output 4."],"answer":"Domain $\\{1,2,3\\}$; co-domain $\\{4,9,16\\}$; range $\\{4,9\\}$.","model":null},{"q":"Find the equation of the line through $(-2,7)$ and $(4,-5)$.","steps":["$m=\\dfrac{-5-7}{4-(-2)}=\\dfrac{-12}{6}=-2$.","$y=-2x+c$; at $(-2,7)$: $7=4+c$, so $c=3$.","Check at $(4,-5)$: $-8+3=-5$ ✓."],"answer":"$y=-2x+3$","model":null},{"q":"For $x=0,1,2,3$ the outputs are $7,\\ 14,\\ 28,\\ 56$. <script type="application/json" id="pack-y1w13">{"year":1,"week":13,"id":"y1w13","title":"Straight Lines, Gradient, Distance and Graphs","subtitle":"Plotting points, measuring steepness, writing the equation of a line, and finding distances and midpoints on the coordinate plane.","family":"geometry","section":{"no":3,"name":"Geometry and Measurement","strand":"Geometry Around Us","from":13,"to":20},"outcomes":["Plot and read ordered pairs in all four quadrants of the Cartesian plane.","Calculate the gradient of a straight line from two points, from a graph or from its equation.","Write the equation of a line in the forms $y=mx+c$, $y-y_1=m(x-x_1)$ and $ax+by+c=0$.","Use gradients to decide whether two lines are parallel or perpendicular.","Find the distance between two points and the midpoint of a line segment.","Interpret the gradient and intercept of a straight-line graph in a real situation."],"keywords":["Cartesian plane","ordered pair","quadrant","gradient","intercept","parallel","perpendicular","distance","midpoint"],"notes":[{"title":"The Cartesian plane and ordered pairs","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"The **Cartesian plane** is made by two perpendicular number lines. The horizontal line is the $x$-axis and the vertical line is the $y$-axis. They cross at the **origin** $O(0,0)$. The axes divide the plane into four **quadrants**, numbered anticlockwise from the top right."},{"k":"box","kind":"definition","title":"Ordered pair","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"A point is named by an **ordered pair** $(x,y)$. The first number, $x$, tells you how far to move horizontally from the origin (right if positive, left if negative). The second number, $y$, tells you how far to move vertically (up if positive, down if negative)."}]},{"k":"p","text":"For example, to plot $B(-3,2)$, start at the origin, move 3 units **left** and then 2 units **up**."},{"k":"fig","id":"w13-plane","caption":"The four quadrants. The signs of the coordinates tell you which quadrant a point is in."},{"k":"box","kind":"warn","title":"Order matters","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"$(3,2)$ and $(2,3)$ are different points. Always write the horizontal coordinate first. Label both axes and use an even scale on each axis."}]}],"figs":["w13-plane"]},{"title":"What the gradient measures","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"The **gradient** (or slope) of a line tells us how steep it is: it is the change in $y$ for every increase of 1 unit in $x$. On a straight line the gradient is the same everywhere, so we can measure it between any two points on the line."},{"k":"box","kind":"formula","title":"Gradient of the line through $A(x_1,y_1)$ and $B(x_2,y_2)$","blocks":[{"k":"math","tex":"m=\\frac{\\text{rise}}{\\text{run}}=\\frac{y_2-y_1}{x_2-x_1},\\qquad x_2\\neq x_1"}]},{"k":"fig","id":"w13-gradient","caption":"Between $A$ and $B$ the line rises 4 units while it runs 4 units across, so $m=\\frac{4}{4}=1$."},{"k":"p","text":"Subtract in the **same order** on the top and on the bottom: if you start with $y_2$ on the top, start with $x_2$ on the bottom."},{"k":"fig","id":"w13-four-gradients","caption":"A line that rises from left to right has a positive gradient; one that falls has a negative gradient. A horizontal line has gradient $0$. A vertical line has no gradient because its run is $0$."},{"k":"box","kind":"key","title":"Parallel and perpendicular lines","blocks":[{"k":"ul","items":["Two non-vertical lines are **parallel** when their gradients are equal: $m_1=m_2$.","Two lines (neither of them horizontal nor vertical) are **perpendicular** when $m_1m_2=-1$, that is, $m_2=-\\dfrac{1}{m_1}$."]}]},{"k":"fig","id":"w13-parallel-perp","caption":"The two blue lines have the same gradient $\\frac{1}{2}$, so they are parallel. The red line has gradient $-2$, and $\\frac{1}{2}\\times(-2)=-1$, so it is perpendicular to both."}],"figs":["w13-gradient","w13-four-gradients","w13-parallel-perp"]},{"title":"Three forms of the equation of a line","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"Every straight line (except a vertical one) can be written in the **gradient–intercept form** $y=mx+c$, where $m$ is the gradient and $c$ is the $y$-intercept."},{"k":"box","kind":"formula","title":"Equations of a straight line","blocks":[{"k":"ul","items":["**Gradient–intercept form:** $y=mx+c$","**Point–gradient form:** $y-y_1=m(x-x_1)$","**General form:** $ax+by+c=0$"]}]},{"k":"p","text":"To find the equation of the line through two points, first find the gradient, then substitute one of the points into $y-y_1=m(x-x_1)$ and simplify. The three forms describe the same line; you can move from one to another by rearranging."},{"k":"box","kind":"tip","title":"Check your equation","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"Substitute both given points into your final equation. If either point does not fit, there is an error."}]}],"figs":[]},{"title":"Intercepts and drawing a line","blocks":[{"k":"ul","items":["The **$x$-intercept** is where the line meets the $x$-axis. Put $y=0$ and solve for $x$.","The **$y$-intercept** is where the line meets the $y$-axis. Put $x=0$ and solve for $y$."]},{"k":"p","text":"For $3x+2y=12$: when $y=0$, $3x=12$ so $x=4$; when $x=0$, $2y=12$ so $y=6$. Two points are enough to draw a straight line; a third point is a useful check."},{"k":"table","head":["$x$","$0$","$2$","$4$"],"rows":[["$y=\\dfrac{12-3x}{2}$","$6$","$3$","$0$"]]},{"k":"fig","id":"w13-intercepts","caption":"The line $3x+2y=12$ crosses the axes at $(4,0)$ and $(0,6)$. The point $(2,3)$ also lies on it."}],"figs":["w13-intercepts"]},{"title":"Distance and midpoint","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"The horizontal and vertical changes between two points form the two shorter sides of a right-angled triangle. Pythagoras’ theorem then gives the length of the segment."},{"k":"box","kind":"formula","title":"Distance and midpoint of $A(x_1,y_1)$ and $B(x_2,y_2)$","blocks":[{"k":"math","tex":"AB=\\sqrt{(x_2-x_1)^2+(y_2-y_1)^2}"},{"k":"math","tex":"M=\\left(\\frac{x_1+x_2}{2},\\ \\frac{y_1+y_2}{2}\\right)"}]},{"k":"fig","id":"w13-distance","caption":"From $A(-5,2)$ to $B(7,7)$: $\\Delta x=12$ and $\\Delta y=5$, so $AB=\\sqrt{12^2+5^2}=13$. The midpoint $M$ is halfway along both directions."},{"k":"p","text":"A distance is a length and has units (for example metres). A midpoint is a **point**, so write it as a coordinate pair."}],"figs":["w13-distance"]},{"title":"Straight-line graphs in real life","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"Many everyday relationships are linear. In a **distance–time graph** the gradient is the speed. In a **cost graph** the gradient is the extra cost of one more unit, and the vertical intercept is a fixed charge that you pay even before any units are used."},{"k":"fig","id":"w13-cost","caption":"A phone repairer charges a fixed GH₵25 plus GH₵12 per hour. The graph starts at 25 and rises 12 for every hour."},{"k":"box","kind":"life","title":"Reading a graph in context","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"For the repair bill $C=12t+25$: the gradient $12$ means each extra hour adds GH₵12, and the intercept $25$ is the inspection fee. After 4 hours the bill is $C=12(4)+25=73$, that is, GH₵73."}]},{"k":"box","kind":"warn","title":"Common errors","blocks":[{"k":"ul","items":["Mixing the order of subtraction in the gradient formula.","Writing $(y,x)$ instead of $(x,y)$.","Saying a vertical line has gradient $0$ (it is a **horizontal** line that has gradient $0$).","Leaving out units in a distance, or writing a midpoint as a single number."]}]}],"figs":["w13-cost"]}],"examples":[{"title":"Gradient between two bus stops","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"On a road map, two bus stops are at $A(-2,3)$ and $B(4,-9)$. Find the gradient of the straight road joining them and explain what its sign means."}],"steps":["Let $(x_1,y_1)=(-2,3)$ and $(x_2,y_2)=(4,-9)$.","Substitute into the gradient formula: $m=\\frac{y_2-y_1}{x_2-x_1}=\\frac{-9-3}{4-(-2)}=\\frac{-12}{6}=-2$","The gradient is negative, so the road falls from left to right: it goes down 2 units for every 1 unit to the right."],"answer":"$m=-2$","figs":[]},{"title":"Equation of the line through two points","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"Find the equation of the straight line through $P(2,-1)$ and $Q(6,7)$. Write it in the form $y=mx+c$ and check both points."}],"steps":["Gradient: $m=\\frac{7-(-1)}{6-2}=\\frac{8}{4}=2$","Use $y-y_1=m(x-x_1)$ with $P(2,-1)$: $y-(-1)=2(x-2)\\ \\Longrightarrow\\ y+1=2x-4\\ \\Longrightarrow\\ y=2x-5$","Check $P$: $2(2)-5=-1$ ✓. Check $Q$: $2(6)-5=7$ ✓."],"answer":"$y=2x-5$","figs":[]},{"title":"From a gradient and a point to the general form","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"A line has gradient $-\\dfrac{3}{4}$ and passes through $(-4,5)$. Find its equation in the form $ax+by+c=0$ with integer coefficients."}],"steps":["Point–gradient form: $y-5=-\\frac{3}{4}(x+4)$","Multiply both sides by $4$ to clear the fraction: $4y-20=-3x-12$.","Collect all terms on the left: $3x+4y-8=0$.","Check with $(-4,5)$: $3(-4)+4(5)-8=-12+20-8=0$ ✓."],"answer":"$3x+4y-8=0$","figs":[]},{"title":"Distance and midpoint on a field","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"A farmer marks two corners of a field at $A(-5,2)$ and $B(7,7)$ on a grid measured in metres. Find the distance $AB$ and the midpoint of $AB$."}],"steps":["Horizontal change: $\\Delta x=7-(-5)=12$ m. Vertical change: $\\Delta y=7-2=5$ m.","By Pythagoras: $AB=\\sqrt{12^2+5^2}=\\sqrt{144+25}=\\sqrt{169}=13\\ \\text{m}$","Midpoint: $M=\\left(\\frac{-5+7}{2},\\ \\frac{2+7}{2}\\right)=\\left(1,\\ \\frac{9}{2}\\right)=(1,\\ 4.5)$"],"answer":"$AB=13$ m and $M(1,\\ 4.5)$","figs":[]},{"title":"Parallel or perpendicular?","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"Two straight roads have equations $2x-3y+6=0$ and $y=kx-4$. Find $k$ if the roads are (a) parallel, (b) perpendicular."}],"steps":["Make $y$ the subject of the first equation: $-3y=-2x-6$, so $y=\\dfrac{2}{3}x+2$. Its gradient is $m_1=\\dfrac{2}{3}$.","(a) Parallel lines have equal gradients, so $k=\\dfrac{2}{3}$.","(b) Perpendicular lines satisfy $m_1k=-1$: $\\frac{2}{3}k=-1\\ \\Longrightarrow\\ k=-\\frac{3}{2}$"],"answer":"(a) $k=\\dfrac{2}{3}$ (b) $k=-\\dfrac{3}{2}$","figs":[]},{"title":"A linear cost function","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"A phone repairer charges a fixed inspection fee of GH₵25 plus GH₵12 for each hour of work. Write the bill $C$ (in cedis) in terms of the time $t$ (in hours), find the bill for 4 hours, and explain the gradient and the intercept."}],"steps":["The labour charge is $12t$ and the fixed fee is $25$, so $C=12t+25$.","For 4 hours: $C=12(4)+25=48+25=73$.","The gradient $12$ is the cost of each extra hour (GH₵12 per hour). The intercept $25$ is the bill when $t=0$: the inspection fee."],"answer":"$C=12t+25$; the bill for 4 hours is GH₵73.","figs":[]},{"title":"Using an intercept","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"A line passes through $(2,9)$ and meets the $x$-axis at $(-1,0)$. Find its equation and its $y$-intercept."}],"steps":["Gradient: $m=\\frac{9-0}{2-(-1)}=\\frac{9}{3}=3$","Using $(-1,0)$: $y-0=3(x+1)$, so $y=3x+3$.","On the $y$-axis $x=0$, so $y=3$."],"answer":"$y=3x+3$; the $y$-intercept is $3$.","figs":[]},{"title":"Finding an unknown coordinate","problem":[{"k":"p","text":"The distance between $(k,1)$ and $(5,4)$ is 5 units. Find all possible values of $k$."}],"steps":["Distance formula: $5=\\sqrt{(5-k)^2+(4-1)^2}$","Square both sides: $25=(5-k)^2+9$, so $(5-k)^2=16$.","Then $5-k=4$ or $5-k=-4$, giving $k=1$ or $k=9$.","Check: in both cases the horizontal change is $4$ and the vertical change is $3$, and $\\sqrt{4^2+3^2}=5$ ✓."],"answer":"$k=1$ or $k=9$","figs":[]}],"summary":[{"title":"Key results for Week 13","items":["Gradient: $m=\\dfrac{y_2-y_1}{x_2-x_1}$","Line with gradient $m$ and $y$-intercept $c$: $y=mx+c$","Line through $(x_1,y_1)$ with gradient $m$: $y-y_1=m(x-x_1)$","Distance: $AB=\\sqrt{(x_2-x_1)^2+(y_2-y_1)^2}$","Midpoint: $M=\\left(\\dfrac{x_1+x_2}{2},\\ \\dfrac{y_1+y_2}{2}\\right)$"]}],"quiz":[{"q":"The gradient of the line through $(-1,4)$ and $(3,-4)$ is","options":["$2$","$-2$","$-\\dfrac{1}{2}$","$-4$"],"correct":1,"explain":"The vertical change is $-4-4=-8$ and the horizontal change is $3-(-1)=4$, so $m=\\dfrac{-8}{4}=-2$."},{"q":"Which equation has gradient $3$ and passes through $(0,-2)$?","options":["$y=3x+2$","$y=-2x+3$","$y=3x-2$","$y=-3x-2$"],"correct":2,"explain":"The gradient $3$ gives $m=3$ and the point $(0,-2)$ is the $y$-intercept, so $y=3x-2$."},{"q":"The midpoint of $(-6,5)$ and $(2,-3)$ is","options":["$(-2,1)$","$(4,2)$","$(-4,-2)$","$(2,-1)$"],"correct":0,"explain":"Average each coordinate: $\\left(\\dfrac{-6+2}{2},\\dfrac{5+(-3)}{2}\\right)=(-2,1)$."},{"q":"The distance between $(0,0)$ and $(8,6)$ is","options":["$14$","$8$","$6$","$10$"],"correct":3,"explain":"$\\sqrt{8^2+6^2}=\\sqrt{64+36}=\\sqrt{100}=10$."},{"q":"The line $4x+2y-7=0$ has gradient","options":["$2$","$-2$","$\\dfrac{1}{2}$","$-\\dfrac{1}{2}$"],"correct":1,"explain":"Rearrange: $2y=-4x+7$, so $y=-2x+\\dfrac{7}{2}$ and $m=-2$."},{"q":"A line perpendicular to a line of gradient $-\\dfrac{5}{2}$ has gradient","options":["$-\\dfrac{2}{5}$","$\\dfrac{2}{5}$","$\\dfrac{5}{2}$","$-\\dfrac{5}{2}$"],"correct":1,"explain":"Perpendicular gradients multiply to $-1$: $-\\dfrac{5}{2}\\times\\dfrac{2}{5}=-1$."},{"q":"Which point lies on $y=2x+1$?","options":["$(2,4)$","$(1,1)$","$(-1,-1)$","$(0,2)$"],"correct":2,"explain":"When $x=-1$, $y=2(-1)+1=-1$. The other points do not satisfy the equation."},{"q":"The $x$-intercept of $3x+2y=12$ is","options":["$(0,6)$","$(6,0)$","$(0,4)$","$(4,0)$"],"correct":3,"explain":"Put $y=0$: $3x=12$, so $x=4$. The intercept is the point $(4,0)$."},{"q":"The horizontal line through $(3,7)$ has equation","options":["$x=3$","$y=7$","$y=3$","$x=7$"],"correct":1,"explain":"Every point on a horizontal line has the same $y$-coordinate, here $7$."},{"q":"A taxi charges GH₵10 plus GH₵4 per kilometre. The cost of a 7 km journey is","options":["GH₵38","GH₵28","GH₵74","GH₵17"],"correct":0,"explain":"$C=10+4\\times7=10+28=38$ cedis."}],"exercise":[{"q":"Find the equation of the line joining $(-3,8)$ and $(5,-4)$, and state its intercepts.","a":"$m=-\\dfrac{3}{2}$, so $y=-\\dfrac{3}{2}x+\\dfrac{7}{2}$, or $3x+2y-7=0$. Intercepts: $\\left(\\dfrac{7}{3},0\\right)$ and $\\left(0,\\dfrac{7}{2}\\right)$."},{"q":"A triangular plot has vertices $(1,2)$, $(7,2)$ and $(4,6)$. Find the three side lengths and classify the triangle.","a":"The sides are $6$, $5$ and $5$ units, so the triangle is isosceles."},{"q":"Find $k$ if the line $2x+ky=6$ is perpendicular to $y=-3x+8$.","a":"The first line has gradient $-\\dfrac{2}{k}$; $\\left(-\\dfrac{2}{k}\\right)(-3)=-1$ gives $k=-6$."},{"q":"A school bus charges GH₵8 plus GH₵2.50 per kilometre. How far did a learner travel if the fare was GH₵43?","a":"$8+2.5d=43$, so $2.5d=35$ and $d=14$ km."},{"q":"A line through $(k,2)$ and $(4,8)$ has gradient $2$. Find $k$ and the equation of the line.","a":"$\\dfrac{8-2}{4-k}=2$ gives $k=1$; the line is $y=2x$."},{"q":"Find the gradient and the $y$-intercept of the line $5x-2y+4=0$.","a":"$y=\\dfrac{5}{2}x+2$, so $m=\\dfrac{5}{2}$ and the $y$-intercept is $2$."},{"q":"Find the midpoint and the length of $PQ$, where $P(-2,-1)$ and $Q(4,7)$.","a":"Midpoint $(1,3)$; $PQ=\\sqrt{6^2+8^2}=10$ units."},{"q":"Show that the points $(0,-1)$, $(2,3)$ and $(5,9)$ lie on one straight line.","a":"Both gradients equal $2$ and the segments share $(2,3)$, so the points are collinear (on $y=2x-1$)."}],"theory":[{"q":"The points $P(-2,-3)$, $Q(1,3)$ and $R(4,9)$ are marked on a map grid. Show that the three points lie on one straight line, and find the equation of that line.","steps":["Gradient of $PQ$: $m_{PQ}=\\dfrac{3-(-3)}{1-(-2)}=\\dfrac{6}{3}=2$.","Gradient of $QR$: $m_{QR}=\\dfrac{9-3}{4-1}=\\dfrac{6}{3}=2$.","The gradients are equal and the segments share the point $Q$, so $P$, $Q$ and $R$ are collinear.","Using $Q(1,3)$: $y-3=2(x-1)$, so $y=2x+1$.","Check: $2(-2)+1=-3$ for $P$ and $2(4)+1=9$ for $R$."],"answer":"The points are collinear; the line is $y=2x+1$.","model":null},{"q":"Find the equation of the line through $(3,-2)$ that is perpendicular to $2x+5y-10=0$. Give the answer in the form $ax+by+c=0$ with integer coefficients.","steps":["Rearrange: $5y=-2x+10$, so $y=-\\dfrac{2}{5}x+2$ and $m_1=-\\dfrac{2}{5}$.","Perpendicular gradient: $m_2=\\dfrac{5}{2}$, because $-\\dfrac{2}{5}\\times\\dfrac{5}{2}=-1$.","Point–gradient form: $y+2=\\dfrac{5}{2}(x-3)$.","Multiply by 2: $2y+4=5x-15$, so $5x-2y-19=0$.","Check: $5(3)-2(-2)-19=15+4-19=0$."],"answer":"$5x-2y-19=0$","model":null},{"q":"Show that the triangle with vertices $A(1,2)$, $B(5,5)$ and $C(2,9)$ has a right angle at $B$. Confirm this using side lengths, then find its area.","steps":["$m_{AB}=\\dfrac{5-2}{5-1}=\\dfrac{3}{4}$ and $m_{BC}=\\dfrac{9-5}{2-5}=-\\dfrac{4}{3}$.","$m_{AB}\\times m_{BC}=\\dfrac{3}{4}\\times\\left(-\\dfrac{4}{3}\\right)=-1$, so $AB\\perp BC$ and $\\angle ABC=90^\\circ$.","Lengths: $AB=\\sqrt{4^2+3^2}=5$, $BC=\\sqrt{(-3)^2+4^2}=5$, $AC=\\sqrt{1^2+7^2}=\\sqrt{50}$.","Check: $AB^2+BC^2=25+25=50=AC^2$, as Pythagoras’ theorem requires.","Area $=\\dfrac{1}{2}\\times AB\\times BC=\\dfrac{1}{2}\\times5\\times5=12.5$ square units."],"answer":"Right angle at $B$; area $12.5$ square units.","model":null},{"q":"$M(3,-1)$ is the midpoint of $PQ$, where $P$ is the point $(-1,4)$. Find the coordinates of $Q$ and the exact length of $PQ$.","steps":["Let $Q=(x,y)$. Then $\\dfrac{-1+x}{2}=3$ and $\\dfrac{4+y}{2}=-1$.","So $x=7$ and $y=-6$, giving $Q(7,-6)$.","$PQ=\\sqrt{(7-(-1))^2+(-6-4)^2}=\\sqrt{64+100}=\\sqrt{164}$.","Simplify: $\\sqrt{164}=\\sqrt{4\\times41}=2\\sqrt{41}\\approx12.81$ units."],"answer":"$Q(7,-6)$ and $PQ=2\\sqrt{41}\\approx12.81$ units.","model":null},{"q":"A water tank is drained at a steady rate. After 2 minutes it holds 340 litres; after 7 minutes it holds 190 litres. Find a linear model $V=mt+c$, explain the meaning of $m$ and $c$, and find when the tank will be empty.","steps":["Gradient: $m=\\dfrac{190-340}{7-2}=\\dfrac{-150}{5}=-30$ litres per minute.","Substitute $(2,340)$: $340=-30(2)+c$, so $c=400$. The model is $V=-30t+400$.","The gradient $-30$ means the volume falls by 30 litres every minute; the intercept $400$ is the volume when draining started.","Empty when $V=0$: $-30t+400=0$, so $t=\\dfrac{400}{30}=13\\tfrac{1}{3}$ minutes (13 minutes 20 seconds)."],"answer":"$V=-30t+400$; the tank is empty after $13\\tfrac{1}{3}$ minutes.","model":null}],"checklist":["I can plot and read points in all four quadrants.","I can find the gradient of a line from two points or from its equation.","I can write the equation of a line in the forms $y=mx+c$ and $ax+by+c=0$.","I can find the $x$- and $y$-intercepts of a line.","I can use gradients to recognise parallel and perpendicular lines.","I can find the distance between two points and the midpoint of a segment.","I can explain what the gradient and intercept mean in a real situation."],"plan":{"lessons":[[{"j":0,"notes":true,"exs":[]},{"j":1,"notes":true,"exs":[0]},{"j":2,"notes":true,"exs":[1,2]}],[{"j":2,"notes":false,"exs":[3,4,5,6]},{"j":3,"notes":true,"exs":[]},{"j":4,"notes":true,"exs":[7]},{"j":5,"notes":true,"exs":[]}]],"exSec":[1,2,2,2,2,2,2,4],"quizSec":[1,2,4,4,1,1,2,3,2,5],"exerSec":[2,2,1,5,2,3,4,1],"thSec":[2,2,4,4,5],"sumSec":[1,3,1,4,4],"chkSec":[0,2,2,3,1,4,5],"weights":[1190.6,2422.75,5082.45,722.9000000000001,1512.4,1171.35],"figs":[{"id":"w13-plane","sec":0,"lesson":1,"caption":"The four quadrants. Bisecting it gives $30^\\circ$."}]}],"figs":["w14-bisect"]},{"title":"Angle relationships","blocks":[{"k":"fig","id":"w14-relations","caption":"Four important facts about angles."},{"k":"box","kind":"formula","title":"Four angle facts","blocks":[{"k":"ul","items":["**Complementary** angles add up to $90^\\circ$.","**Supplementary** angles add up to $180^\\circ$. Conversely, if a pair of corresponding angles is equal, the lines must be parallel."}]},{"k":"p","text":"**Perpendicular** lines meet at $90^\\circ$."}],"figs":["w14-transversal","w14-pairs"]},{"title":"Angles in algebra","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"Many questions give angles as expressions such as $(3x+12)^\\circ$."},{"k":"ol","items":["Decide which angle fact applies (equal, adds to $90^\\circ$, $180^\\circ$ or $360^\\circ$).","Write an equation and solve it for $x$.","Substitute to find the actual angles, and check that they fit the diagram (an “acute” angle cannot be $122^\\circ$)."]},{"k":"box","kind":"tip","title":"Give a reason for every step","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"Write the angle fact next to each line, for example “vertically opposite angles are equal” or “co-interior angles, $l_1\\parallel l_2$”. A **vector** has both **magnitude and direction**, for example displacement, velocity and force."},{"k":"p","text":"“A boat travels 10 km” gives a distance (a scalar). “A boat travels 10 km due east” gives a displacement (a vector)."},{"k":"p","text":"A vector is drawn as an arrow: the **tail** is the starting point, the **head** is the end point, and the length shows the magnitude to scale. $\\overrightarrow{AB}$ means the journey **from** $A$ **to** $B$."}],"figs":[]},{"title":"Column vectors and components","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"On a grid, a vector is described by how far it moves **across** and **up**. We write it as a **column vector**:"},{"k":"math","tex":"\\overrightarrow{AB}=\\cv{4}{3}\\qquad\\text{(4 units right, 3 units up)}"},{"k":"fig","id":"w17-vector","caption":"$\\overrightarrow{AB}=\\cv{4}{3}$: 4 units across and 3 units up. Its length is 5 units."},{"k":"box","kind":"formula","title":"The vector from $A$ to $B$","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"For $A(x_1,y_1)$ and $B(x_2,y_2)$:"},{"k":"math","tex":"\\overrightarrow{AB}=\\begin{pmatrix}x_2-x_1\\\\y_2-y_1\\end{pmatrix}"},{"k":"p","text":"Always subtract the **start** from the **end**."}]},{"k":"p","text":"In $\\cv{p}{q}$, $p$ is the horizontal component (positive to the right or east, negative to the left or west) and $q$ is the vertical component (positive up or north, negative down or south). Some books write the same vector as $(p,q)$."}],"figs":["w17-vector"]},{"title":"Magnitude and direction","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"A vector $\\cv{p}{q}$ is the hypotenuse of a right-angled triangle with legs $|p|$ and $|q|$, so by Pythagoras’ theorem:"},{"k":"box","kind":"formula","title":"Magnitude of a vector","blocks":[{"k":"math","tex":"\\left|\\cv{p}{q}\\right|=\\sqrt{p^2+q^2}"},{"k":"p","text":"The magnitude is never negative."}]},{"k":"p","text":"For a vector pointing up and to the right ($p>0$, $q>0$), the angle $\\theta$ above the positive $x$-axis satisfies $\\tan\\theta=\\dfrac{q}{p}$. In other quadrants, use a sketch to decide the direction."},{"k":"p","text":"A **unit vector** has magnitude $1$. To get the unit vector in the direction of $\\mathbf{v}$, divide by its magnitude: $\\hat{\\mathbf{v}}=\\dfrac{\\mathbf{v}}{|\\mathbf{v}|}$."}],"figs":[]},{"title":"Kinds of vectors","blocks":[{"k":"fig","id":"w17-kinds","caption":"Equal vectors have the same components wherever they are drawn; $-\\mathbf{a}$ points the opposite way; $\\tfrac{1}{2}\\mathbf{a}$ is parallel to $\\mathbf{a}$ and half as long."},{"k":"ul","items":["**Equal vectors** have the same components (same magnitude and direction), even if they are drawn in different places.","The **negative** $-\\mathbf{a}$ has the same magnitude as $\\mathbf{a}$ but the opposite direction: $-\\cv{3}{-4}=\\cv{-3}{4}$.","The **zero vector** $\\cv{0}{0}$ has no length and no direction.","**Parallel vectors** are multiples of each other: $\\mathbf{u}=k\\mathbf{v}$ with $k\\neq0$. If $k>0$ they point the same way; if $k<0$ they point in opposite directions. Parallel does not mean equal."]}],"figs":["w17-kinds"]},{"title":"Adding and subtracting vectors","blocks":[{"k":"box","kind":"formula","title":"Vector operations","blocks":[{"k":"math","tex":"\\cv{a}{b}+\\cv{c}{d}=\\cv{a+c}{b+d}\\qquad\\cv{a}{b}-\\cv{c}{d}=\\cv{a-c}{b-d}\\qquad k\\cv{a}{b}=\\cv{ka}{kb}"}]},{"k":"p","text":"The **triangle law**: going from $A$ to $B$ and then from $B$ to $C$ has the same overall effect as going straight from $A$ to $C$:"},{"k":"math","tex":"\\overrightarrow{AB}+\\overrightarrow{BC}=\\overrightarrow{AC}"},{"k":"fig","id":"w17-triangle","caption":"The resultant $\\overrightarrow{AC}$ joins the start of the first vector to the end of the second."},{"k":"box","kind":"key","title":"Distance and displacement","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"**Distance** is the total length of the route (a scalar). **Displacement** is the straight-line change from start to finish (a vector). Walking 3 km east and then 3 km west covers 6 km, but the displacement is zero."}]}],"figs":["w17-triangle"]},{"title":"Bearings","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"A **true bearing** is measured **from north**, **clockwise**, and written with **three digits**: north is $000^\\circ$, east $090^\\circ$, south $180^\\circ$ and west $270^\\circ$."},{"k":"fig","id":"w17-compass","caption":"A bearing of $065^\\circ$ is a clockwise turn of $65^\\circ$ from north. The back bearing is $065^\\circ+180^\\circ=245^\\circ$."},{"k":"box","kind":"formula","title":"Back bearings","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"The **back bearing** (the direction for the return journey) is"},{"k":"ul","items":["the bearing $+\\,180^\\circ$ if the bearing is less than $180^\\circ$;","the bearing $-\\,180^\\circ$ if the bearing is $180^\\circ$ or more."]}]},{"k":"p","text":"**Compass directions** such as N$40^\\circ$W start at north or south and turn towards east or west."},{"k":"fig","id":"w17-convert","caption":"N$40^\\circ$W is the bearing $320^\\circ$; S$25^\\circ$E is the bearing $155^\\circ$."},{"k":"box","kind":"warn","title":"Two different angle systems","blocks":[{"k":"p","text":"True bearings are measured **clockwise from north**.
